newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Bank of Ireland pft seen up 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bank of Ireland pft seen up 10 pct.

text.p: Bank of Ireland Plc, one of Ireland's largest financial services groups, is expected on Wednesday to announce a 10 percent gain in annual profit and raise its total dividend by between 15 and 18 percent.

Analysts say the bank, which last year bought Britain's Bristol & West building society, will report pretax profit rose to around 400 million Irish pounds ($608 million) in the year to end-March from 363.7 million in the previous year.
The results are expected around 0630 GMT.

Growth will have been tempered by the bank's desire to maintain prudent capital ratios after the Bristol & West acquisition, which cost 600 million sterling. But the impact will not have been dramatic and retail business in Ireland remains buoyant, analysts said.

"After Bristol & West, they would have been very aware of what they need their balance sheet to be in order to maintain capital ratios. To a certain extent that would have restricted loan growth on the retail side. Beyond that, I don't expect any nasties," one Dublin-based analyst said.
Analysts said the desire to build up the balance sheet explained what was likely to be cautious dividend cover of around three times earnings.

Riada Stockbrokers, which recommends Bank of Ireland shares as a "hold" and sees annual pretax profit at 400 million pounds and earnings per share of 51.8p, is predicting an 18p net total dividend, up from 15.25p.
Goodbody Stockbrokers in Dublin sees the payout marginally lower at 17.5p on expected pretax profit of 404.5 million and earnings per share of 52p.

"Now we have seen the fair-value adjustments they are applying to the Bristol & West balance sheet, the goodwill write-off is a 100 million pounds more than I was predicting ...and that might explain why they are being judicious about using their capital," said Oliver O'Shea at Goodbody.

O'Shea said the bank appeared to be behaving as if it had a capital constraint. But he said the company had no need to raise capital because there was still considerable credit demand in the Irish economy. Also, the bank's return on equity of around 20 percent meant it could build up capital ratios quickly.

"The Bank of Ireland is unusual with dividend cover of three times so basically it is retaining two thirds of its profit on the balance sheet...Most banks cover between two and two and half times. Now that Bristol and West is on the table they will be running down their surplus and may stick with three times cover," O'Shea said.
Bank of Ireland paid cash for Bristol & West, one of Britain's top ten building societies. Last November, its chief executive Pat Molloy said the bank would focus on building up capital.
In the six months to September 30, 1996, the bank raised pretax profit to 193.1 million Irish pounds from 191.8 million and paid an interim dividend of 6.1p.
